"Move as one body" means the collision is **perfectly inelastic**, so momentum alone
decides the answer.
**Step 1 — set a sign convention.** Take the direction of the 10 m s⁻¹ body as
**positive**, so the other, moving the opposite way, is **−7 m s⁻¹**.
**Step 2 — find the total momentum before.**
p = (40)(+10) + (40)(−7)
= 400 − 280
= **120 kg m s⁻¹**
**Step 3 — apply conservation of momentum.** After the collision the two move together
as a single body of mass 40 + 40 = **80 kg**:
80 v = 120
**v = 1·5 m s⁻¹** ✓
in the direction of the **faster** body ✓
**Why momentum and not energy.** Bodies that stick together have had a **perfectly
inelastic** collision, in which kinetic energy is **not** conserved ✓ Momentum is
conserved in every collision, so it is the only usable principle here.
**How much energy is lost.**
before: ½(40)(10²) + ½(40)(7²) = 2000 + 980 = **2980 J**
after: ½(80)(1·5²) = **90 J**
lost: **2890 J** — about 97% of it, converted to heat and deformation ✓ an enormous loss,
which is what happens when two nearly equal, nearly opposite momenta cancel.
**A note on the wording.** The question says "collide-elastically, and move as one body",
which is self-contradictory: an **elastic** collision conserves kinetic energy and the
bodies separate, while moving as one body is the perfectly **inelastic** case ✓ The phrase
"move as one body" is decisive and is what the options are built on — the elastic reading
would give two different final velocities, not one.
**Reading the distractors.**
**3 m s⁻¹** ✗ would follow from (10 − 7)/1 rather than dividing the momentum by the total
mass — that is, forgetting that the combined mass is 80 kg, not 40.
**10 m s⁻¹** and **7 m s⁻¹** ✗ are the original speeds; the combination must be **slower**
than either, since the two momenta largely cancel ✓
That last check settles it immediately: the answer has to be well below 7.
∴ 1·5 m/s.

The **angle of friction** is defined as the angle the **resultant** of the normal force
and the limiting friction makes with the normal — and its tangent is μ.
**Step 1 — draw the two contact forces.** A surface exerts
the **normal reaction N**, perpendicular to the surface
the **limiting friction f = μN**, along the surface
**Step 2 — find the resultant's direction.** The two are perpendicular, so the resultant
makes an angle θ with the normal where
tan θ = f/N
= μN/N
= **μ**
so
**μ = tan θ** ✓
**What the angle of friction means physically.** It is the greatest angle by which the
total contact force can lean away from the normal ✓ Beyond it the surface cannot supply
enough friction and sliding begins.
**Its link with the angle of repose.** Tilt a plane until a block just begins to slide.
At that angle α,
mg sin α = μ mg cos α, so **μ = tan α**
— the same relation ✓ So the **angle of repose equals the angle of friction**, which is
why the coefficient can be measured simply by tilting a board and noting the angle.
**A worked value.** For μ = 0·5:
θ = tan⁻¹(0·5) = **26·6°**
so a block rests on a 26·6° slope and slides on anything steeper ✓
**Why μ cannot equal θ.** Option (a) equates a **pure number** with an **angle** — two
different kinds of quantity ✗ A coefficient of friction is dimensionless, so it can only
equal a dimensionless function **of** the angle, never the angle itself.
**Why not sin θ or cos θ.** Both are bounded by **1**, but μ can exceed 1 — rubber on dry
tarmac reaches about 1·0 to 1·5, and some clean metals are higher still ✗ Only **tan θ**
can take any value from 0 to infinity, matching the range of μ ✓ That observation alone
rules out options (b) and (c).
**A check at the extremes.** A frictionless surface has μ = 0 and θ = **0°** (the contact
force is purely normal) ✓ and as μ → ∞ the angle approaches **90°** (the surface can
resist any sideways pull) ✓ tan θ behaves exactly so.
∴ μ = tan θ.

Going **down** the slope, gravity pulls the body along the plane while friction, opposing
the motion, acts **up** it — so the two subtract.
**Step 1 — resolve the weight.** On a plane inclined at θ:
component **along** the plane: **mg sin θ** (down the slope)
component **perpendicular**: **mg cos θ**
**Step 2 — find the normal force and the friction.**
N = mg cos θ
f = μN = **μ mg cos θ**
and since the body slides **down**, friction acts **up** the slope ✓
**Step 3 — apply Newton's second law along the plane.**
ma = mg sin θ − μ mg cos θ
**Step 4 — cancel the mass.**
**a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ)** ✓
**Why the mass cancels.** Both the driving force and the friction are proportional to m ✓
so a heavy body and a light one slide down the same slope with the same acceleration —
the same reason all bodies fall at the same rate in free fall.
**The companion case.** A body projected **up** the slope has friction acting **down** it,
so the two **add**:
a = −g(sin θ + μ cos θ)
— a larger deceleration, which is option (b) and the distractor here ✓ Whether the signs
add or subtract depends entirely on the **direction of motion**, since friction always
opposes it.
**When does it slide at all?** Only if mg sin θ exceeds the maximum static friction:
tan θ > μ ✓
If tan θ < μ the body stays put and the acceleration is **zero**, not negative — the
formula applies only once motion has begun.
**A worked value.** With θ = 30°, μ = 0·2 and g = 10 m s⁻²:
a = 10(0·5 − 0·2 × 0·866) = 10(0·5 − 0·173) = **3·27 m s⁻²**
compared with 10(0·5) = **5 m s⁻²** on a smooth slope ✓ friction has taken about a third
of it.
**Reading the other distractors.**
**a = g** ✗ is free fall, which would need a vertical plane and no friction.
**a = g sin θ** ✗ is the **smooth** plane result, with friction ignored — correct only
when μ = 0 ✓
∴ a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ).

**Uniform translatory motion** is motion in which the body as a whole moves without
rotating, at a steady velocity — so every particle of it must do the same thing.
**Step 1 — unpack "translatory".** In **translation**, every line drawn in the body stays
parallel to itself as the body moves ✓ No part turns relative to any other, so every
particle traces an identical path, merely displaced ✓
**Step 2 — unpack "uniform".** Uniform means the velocity is **constant** — constant in
**magnitude and in direction** ✓
**Step 3 — put the two together.** Every particle of the body moves with the **same
velocity**, and that velocity does **not change with time** ✓ That is exactly the third
option.
**Why "same velocity for all particles" is the translation part.** Contrast a rotating
wheel: a point on the rim moves fast, a point near the axle slowly, and the hub not at
all ✓ Different particles have different velocities, so the motion is **not**
translatory. Translation is precisely the case where that difference vanishes.
**Why "unchanging" is the uniform part.** A car accelerating in a straight line is
translatory — all its parts share one velocity at each instant — but **not uniform**,
because that shared velocity keeps growing ✓ Both conditions are needed.
**A test you can apply.** Mark two points on the body and watch the line joining them.
**stays parallel to itself** → translation ✓
**turns** → rotation is present
Then check whether the speed and direction are steady; if so the translation is
**uniform** ✓
**The consequence for forces.** With the velocity constant, the acceleration is zero, so
by Newton's first law the **net force is zero** ✓ The body is in equilibrium even though
it is moving.
**Reading the distractors.** Options describing particles with **different** velocities
✗ describe rotation or general motion; options allowing the velocity to **change** ✗
describe accelerated translation, not uniform translation ✓ Only the statement that **all
particles have the same velocity and it does not change** captures both words in the
phrase.
∴ all particles of the body move with the same, unchanging velocity.

Moving with **uniform velocity** means zero acceleration **and** zero angular
acceleration — so both the net force and the net torque must vanish.
**Step 1 — apply the condition for translation.** Uniform velocity means
a = 0
so by Newton's second law
**F_net = ma = 0** ✓
**Step 2 — apply the condition for rotation.** "Moving with uniform velocity" with no
turning means the angular acceleration is also zero:
**τ_net = Iα = 0** ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** Both the **force and the torque on the scale are zero** ✓
**Why both conditions are needed.** A rigid body has two kinds of motion to account for:
**translation** of its centre of mass, governed by **F_net = ma**
**rotation** about the centre of mass, governed by **τ_net = Iα**
A body can have zero net force yet still spin up — a couple, two equal and opposite
forces along different lines, gives **zero force but non-zero torque** ✓ So zero force
alone does not guarantee uniform motion; the torque condition is independent and must be
stated separately.
**The two equilibrium conditions.** This is exactly **static equilibrium**, extended to a
body already in motion:
ΣF = 0 (no translational acceleration)
Στ = 0 (no angular acceleration)
Together they define **mechanical equilibrium** ✓ A body in uniform motion is in
equilibrium just as surely as one at rest — the first law makes no distinction between
rest and steady motion.
**A concrete picture.** Slide a metre scale across a smooth table so it glides steadily
without spinning. Gravity pulls down, the table pushes up, and these two balance in both
force and moment ✓ Give it a flick on one end instead and the force may still balance,
but the torque does not, and it starts to rotate.
**Reading the distractors.**
**force zero, torque not zero** ✗ would make the scale spin faster and faster, so the
velocity of its ends would not stay uniform.
**torque zero, force not zero** ✗ would accelerate the centre of mass, contradicting
uniform velocity ✓
**both non-zero** ✗ fails on both counts.
∴ force and torque on the scale are both zero.

Friction opposes the **change in velocity**, so it points along **Δv̄ = v̄_final −
v̄_initial** — and the answer follows from drawing that vector.
**Step 1 — write the two velocities.** Take east as +x and north as +y, with speed v
unchanged:
initial, moving **north**: v̄ᵢ = (0, +v)
final, moving **west**: v̄_f = (−v, 0)
**Step 2 — find the change in velocity.**
Δv̄ = v̄_f − v̄ᵢ
= (−v, 0) − (0, +v)
= **(−v, −v)**
**Step 3 — read its direction.** A vector with equal **negative** x and **negative** y
components points **west and south in equal measure** — that is, towards the
**south-west** ✓
**Step 4 — connect force to Δv̄.** The frictional force supplies the acceleration, and
ā = Δv̄/Δt is **parallel** to Δv̄ ✓ So the friction acts along the **south-west**
direction ✓
**Why not along the final direction.** A common instinct is to say the force must point
**west**, the way the player ends up going. But a force along west alone would **add** a
westward velocity while leaving the northward one untouched, giving a north-west motion ✓
The northward component must be **destroyed** as well, and that requires a southward
pull — hence south-**west**, not west.
**The magnitude, for completeness.**
|Δv̄| = √(v² + v²) = **v√2**
so the average force is **mv√2/Δt**, at 45° between south and west ✓
**A check by symmetry.** The turn is through a right angle, and the speed is the same
before and after. The change must therefore be symmetric between "removing the north
motion" and "adding the west motion" — equal parts of each, which is exactly 45°, the
south-west direction ✓
**Reading the distractors.**
**north-east** ✗ is the exact **opposite** of the correct direction — it would speed the
player up towards the north-east, not turn them west.
**north-west** ✗ bisects the initial and final directions, but friction is along the
**difference** of the velocities, not their sum ✓ This is the most tempting wrong answer.
**due west** ✗ ignores the need to cancel the northward motion, as argued above.
**The general rule worth remembering.** For a change of direction at constant speed, the
force points along the **vector difference** of the velocities, which always leans
**backwards** relative to the original motion ✓ Here that backwards lean is the southward
half of south-west.
∴ the frictional force is along the south-west direction.
